analysis.one_liner: Requires all states to offer absentee voting to anyone worried about COVID-19 in the 2020 election.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor in the Senate before the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every state and local election office to let anyone with a reasonable concern about catching COVID-19 register and vote by absentee ballot in the November 2020 election. It would have let the Justice Department sue states that refused, and it authorized about $717 million in federal grants to help election offices build online absentee-ballot request systems, buy postage, envelopes, drop boxes, and ballot-processing equipment, and teach voters how to use absentee ballots.
analysis.who_benefits: Every eligible voter who feared that voting in person during a pandemic would expose them to COVID-19, plus older, disabled, immunocompromised, and essential-working voters who could not safely stand in line. Election offices also benefit from federal funding to run the expanded system.

how_it_helps.text: Each state and local jurisdiction must allow any voter with a reasonable concern about catching COVID-19 at the polls to use absentee registration procedures and vote by absentee ballot in the November 2020 federal election.
The Attorney General may sue a state or local jurisdiction in federal court for declaratory or injunctive relief to enforce the absentee-voting requirement.

The bill authorizes $16.7 million in grants to states for online absentee-ballot request systems and $700 million for the costs of expanded absentee voting, including postage, envelopes, ballot printing, drop boxes, and processing equipment, with at least $200 million reserved for public education about casting and counting absentee ballots.

analysis.who_pays: States and local election offices would bear the operating cost of running a much larger absentee-voting program, offset by the federal grants; federal taxpayers would fund the roughly $717 million in grants; and critics worried a large shift to mail ballots could strain election administration or invite disputes over ballot handling.

drawbacks.text: The federal government would be telling states how to run their own elections for a single election cycle, an intrusion on state election authority that many senators would object to on federalism grounds.

A nationwide shift to absentee voting on this timeline (the bill was introduced June 15, 2020, less than five months before the election) would have required election offices to buy equipment, hire staff, and retrain workers quickly, raising the risk of administrative errors and delays in counting results, which is why the bill reserved $200 million for voter education about how long counting takes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered a direct, time-limited protection: voters who feared infection at the polls could vote from home during a pandemic, with federal money covering most of the cost. Its weaknesses were timing and design. It came late in an election year with a hard deadline, mandated a single election cycle rather than a durable reform, and relied on litigation to force reluctant states to comply. Even a well-run version would have shifted substantial election administration to mail processing with only five months to prepare.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Rules Committee, which never acted on it, and the bill died there when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Senator Merkley introduced the bill on June 15, 2020, and the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Rules and Administration.
No cosponsor ever joined the bill, and the committee took no further action; no hearing, markup, or floor vote occurred before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State officials who wanted no federal mandate on their 2020 election rules were better off, since the requirement and its enforcement never took effect; voters worried about voting in person during the pandemic got no guaranteed federal absentee option, though states remained free to expand absentee access on their own as many did.

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on June 15, 2020, to require pandemic-era absentee voting nationwide.

against.name: Senate Rules and Administration Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on June 15, 2020, and never held a hearing or markup on it.

sides.party_line_note: The bill drew no cosponsors in either party, and with no cosponsor, no hearing, and no vote, the record shows no cross-party support for it.

industries.note: The bill would have imposed a new one-time mandate to process far more absentee ballots, but also sent roughly $717 million in federal grants to pay for materials, drop boxes, equipment, and outreach. Many election officials nationally were asking for exactly this kind of funding in 2020, though the mandate itself would have required rapid changes on short notice.

The bill authorized spending on ballot printing, envelopes, postage, drop boxes, and processing equipment, a one-time surge of purchases that evaporated when the bill died. This is a narrow commercial loss with no direct effect on the public.
